markers.mechanism: Slavic languages lack articles; learners default to bare nouns in English.

examples.input: I went to store to buy book.
examples.output: I went to the store to buy a book.

markers.prompt_hint: Insert 'a', 'an', or 'the' where English requires articles, especially before singular count nouns.

markers.mechanism: Russian present-tense equational sentences omit the verb 'to be'.

examples.output: He is a very good student.

markers.prompt_hint: Add 'is', 'am', or 'are' in present-tense equational and attributive clauses where the speaker dropped the copula.

markers.mechanism: Slavic imperfective aspect is much broader than English continuous; learners over-extend -ing to stative verbs.
markers.prompt_hint: Convert progressive forms of stative verbs (need, know, want, have, believe, understand) to simple present.

markers.mechanism: Russian verb morphology is rich enough to drop subject pronouns; English requires overt subjects.

examples.output: I went to the cinema yesterday.

markers.prompt_hint: Restore dropped subject pronouns (typically 'I', 'we', or 'they') based on context.

markers.mechanism: Russian lacks the 'have something done' periphrastic causative; learners default to active voice.

examples.input: I cut my hair at the salon.
examples.output: I had my hair cut at the salon.

markers.prompt_hint: When the speaker describes an action performed for them by a service provider, restructure to 'have/get X done' if context makes the causative reading clear.

markers.mechanism: Russian punctuation rules forbid the serial (Oxford) comma.
markers.prompt_hint: Add the serial comma before 'and' or 'or' in lists of three or more items.

markers.mechanism: Russian grammar mandates a comma before subordinating что (that); learners transfer this comma into English.

examples.input: He said, that he was tired.
examples.output: He said that he was tired.

markers.prompt_hint: Remove the comma before complementizer 'that' in restrictive subordinate clauses.

markers.mechanism: Russian has no possessive apostrophe; learners drop it in English possessives.
markers.prompt_hint: Insert the possessive apostrophe ('s or s') on possessive nouns.

markers.mechanism: Russian word order is pragmatic (topic-focus driven), not grammatical; learners scramble English SVO order.

examples.input: A new car bought my father.
examples.output: My father bought a new car.

markers.prompt_hint: Restore canonical Subject-Verb-Object order when the speaker has fronted an object or focused element non-standardly.

markers.mechanism: Nouns countable in Russian (advice, information, equipment, knowledge) are uncountable in English.
markers.prompt_hint: Convert plural forms of English mass nouns (advices→advice, informations→information, equipments→equipment, knowledges→knowledge) to singular.

notes: Slavic family: no articles, rich case morphology, perfective/imperfective aspect, pragmatic word order. Patterns also apply (with variation) to Ukrainian and Polish.
